doc.title: Eddie Bert interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: First non-union band at Post Lodge, then Sam Donahue and the union
summary: Playing a Savoy Sultans-style band in Larchmont, then joining the union in a day to go with Sam Donahue.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Wow. That wasn’t actually your first job was it?
So you started, let’s see, you got through high school playing in the school bands and stuff, right? And then it says you went with Sam Donahue? When you were 18?

Well the first band I went with was actually a non-union band. We played at a place called the Post Lodge in Larchmont, New York for about a year, or maybe a year and a half. And what it was, it was three saxes, two trumpets, a trombone and four rhythm. And we played, it was on the style of the Savoy Sultans. And that was seven days a week. And well, I was the only white guy in the band but that’s what I wanted to play, with that kind of music. So that’s what I did. But it was a non-union band and all that. So then all of a sudden I got this offer from Sam Donahue, so I had to join the union, like in one day and go up to Boston and meet him. That’s the way that happened.
Did you have to do anything special to get into the union?
I think they gave me a second trombone part on “Tiger Rag” and see if I could play that.
You know, it was just a formality. But my father knew some violin player that was in the union so he sort of got me in.
Gosh the union played a pretty big role at that time, didn’t it?
Yeah. Because you had to — if you wanted to quit a band, didn’t you have to give a certain amount of notice?
Yeah. But I didn’t have to give any notice because it was a non-union band.
